interactions.label: Which feature most reliably distinguishes dysentery from simple diarrhoea?

params.question: Which feature most reliably distinguishes dysentery from simple diarrhoea?

answers.text: Passage of more than three loose stools per day

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Frequency alone defines diarrhoea, not dysentery. The hallmark of dysentery is mucosal invasion producing blood and mucus, not stool frequency.

answers.text: Passage of bloody, mucoid stools with tenesmus

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Dysentery involves invasion of the colonic mucosa, producing stools containing blood and mucus. Tenesmus — painful, straining urge to defecate — reflects this invasive inflammation.

answers.text: An incubation period of less than six hours after a meal

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: A very short incubation period after a common meal is characteristic of toxin-mediated food poisoning (e.g. staphylococcal enterotoxin), not dysentery.
Fever is typically present in dysentery because the pathogen invades the gut lining and triggers an inflammatory response. Absence of fever would actually argue against dysentery.

overallFeedback.feedback: Review the contrast: diarrhoea is secretory (watery, high-volume, no blood), whereas dysentery is invasive — the pathogen damages the mucosa, producing bloody, mucoid stools with tenesmus and fever.
Well done. The secretory-versus-invasive distinction is the key organising principle: diarrhoea = watery, high-volume, no blood; dysentery = bloody, mucoid, with tenesmus and fever.

interactions.label: What property of Shigella makes it far more contagious than Vibrio cholerae in p

params.question: What property of Shigella makes it far more contagious than Vibrio cholerae in person-to-person transmission?

answers.text: It produces a heat-stable enterotoxin that persists in food

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Heat-stable enterotoxin is associated with ETEC and staphylococcal food poisoning, not with Shigella. Shiga toxin inhibits protein synthesis but is not the reason for high contagiousness.

answers.text: Its extremely low infective dose of just 10 to 100 organisms

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Shigella requires only 10–100 organisms to cause infection, compared with approximately 10⁸ for V. cholerae. This remarkably low dose enables efficient person-to-person spread via the faeco-oral route, especially in crowded settings like schools.

answers.text: It thrives in alkaline water at pH 8.5 to 9

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Alkaline pH tolerance is a characteristic of V. cholerae, which uses this property to survive in environmental water sources. Shigella spreads primarily through direct person-to-person contact.

answers.text: It forms spores that survive for weeks in the environment

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Shigella is a non-spore-forming Gram-negative rod. Its contagiousness comes from an extremely low infective dose, not from environmental persistence through sporulation.

overallFeedback.feedback: The key is the infective dose: Shigella needs only 10–100 organisms, whereas V. cholerae requires approximately 10⁸. This massive difference explains why Shigella spreads person-to-person while cholera spreads mainly through contaminated water.
Exactly. The very low infective dose (10–100 organisms vs 10⁸ for cholera) is why Shigella outbreaks spread so readily through person-to-person contact in crowded settings.

interactions.label: What is the primary role of the urease enzyme produced by Helicobacter pylori in

params.question: What is the primary role of the urease enzyme produced by Helicobacter pylori in establishing gastric infection?

answers.text: It directly disrupts tight junctions between gastric epithelial cells

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Tight junction disruption is the action of the CagA toxin, which is injected into host cells via a type IV secretion system. Urease acts at an earlier, more fundamental step in colonisation.

answers.text: It neutralises gastric acid, creating an alkaline microenvironment for bacterial survival

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Urease hydrolyses urea into ammonia and CO₂. The ammonia buffers the acidic gastric pH around the bacterium, allowing it to survive long enough to adhere to the mucosa. Without this acid-neutralising step, colonisation cannot occur — which is why nearly every diagnostic test for H. pylori exploits urease activity.

answers.text: It acts as a superantigen, triggering massive T-cell activation

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Superantigen activity is characteristic of staphylococcal enterotoxins in food poisoning. H. pylori urease is a metabolic enzyme whose function is acid neutralisation, not immune activation.

answers.text: It functions as an adhesin that binds the bacterium to the gastric epithelium

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Adhesion to the gastric lining is mediated by specific adhesin proteins such as BabA, not by urease. Urease is an enzyme whose function is neutralising stomach acid to enable bacterial survival before adhesion can occur.

overallFeedback.feedback: Urease hydrolyses urea into ammonia, which neutralises the acidic gastric pH around the bacterium. This acid-buffering step enables H. pylori to survive in the stomach — it is the essential prerequisite before adhesins and toxins (CagA, VacA) can take effect.

Exactly. Urease is H. pylori's survival tool — by generating ammonia to neutralise stomach acid, it permits colonisation of the gastric antrum, the essential first step before CagA and VacA can cause tissue damage.

interactions.label: During the 'window period' of acute hepatitis B, which serological finding is ex

params.question: During the 'window period' of acute hepatitis B, which serological finding is expected?

answers.text: Both HBsAg and anti-HBs are detectable simultaneously

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: HBsAg and anti-HBs do not coexist. The window period is precisely the interval between HBsAg disappearing and anti-HBs appearing — neither surface marker is detectable during this gap.

answers.text: HBeAg is at its peak level, indicating maximum viral replication

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: HBeAg peaks during the acute phase while HBsAg is still present, before the window period begins. By the time the window period arrives, HBeAg has typically already declined.

answers.text: Anti-HBc IgM is the sole marker of recent infection

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. In the window period, HBsAg has been cleared but anti-HBs has not yet appeared. Anti-HBc IgM is the only detectable marker, confirming recent acute HBV infection. This is precisely why blood banks test for anti-HBc alongside HBsAg — to catch window-period donors.

answers.text: No serological markers are detectable at all

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: If no markers were detectable, infection would be undiagnosable. Anti-HBc IgM persists through the window period because it targets the core antigen encountered during natural infection, bridging the diagnostic gap.

overallFeedback.feedback: In the window period, HBsAg has been cleared and anti-HBs has not yet appeared. Anti-HBc IgM is the only marker present, making it the essential test for diagnosing acute HBV infection during this interval.
Well done. The window period is a diagnostic gap for surface markers — anti-HBc IgM bridges it and is the only evidence of recent HBV infection during this interval.

params.question: A person who has been successfully vaccinated against hepatitis B will test positive for both anti-HBs and anti-HBc antibodies.

l10n.wrongAnswerMessage: The statement is false. The hepatitis B vaccine is a recombinant subunit vaccine containing only HBsAg — it does not include core antigen. Therefore, a vaccinated person develops only anti-HBs. Anti-HBc requires exposure to the core antigen, which occurs only during natural infection with the whole virus.
l10n.correctAnswerMessage: Correct — the statement is false. The hepatitis B vaccine contains only the surface antigen (HBsAg), so the immune system produces only anti-HBs. Anti-HBc antibodies appear exclusively after natural infection with the whole virus, because core antigen is never part of the vaccine. Finding anti-HBc alongside anti-HBs indicates past natural infection, not vaccination alone.
